papers.core_contribution: This paper summarizes applications of interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and chemistry, discussing how these techniques can improve scientific studies by providing insights beyond predictive power, building trust, and revealing unexpected correlations.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning is crucial for realizing the true potential of ML in materials science, and human experts who embrace interpretable ML will replace those who do not.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in scientific machine learning involves trade-offs between explainability, completeness, and scientific validity (correctness).
Intrinsically interpretable models (e.g., linear models, decision trees) offer direct interpretations but may lack correctness for complex phenomena.
Extrinsic interpretation methods (e.g., SHAP, salience maps, attention mechanisms) can provide insights for complex models like deep neural networks.
Interpretability techniques can generate scientific hypotheses and guide experiments, but they require careful validation to avoid over-interpretation and confusion with causation.
Future directions include integrating uncertainty estimates into explanations and combining machine learning with causal inference for more robust insights.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability methods may lead to over-interpretation, especially when searching for physical explanations, and can be misled by shortcut learning or unrealistic feature combinations.
Explanations from machine learning models do not have strong causal guarantees and are susceptible to confounding effects, requiring secondary confirmation by experiments or simulation.
There is a trade-off between interpretability, completeness, and correctness in model explanations, meaning no single explanation may fully capture the model's operation and physical reality.
future_direction: Integrating uncertainty estimates into model explanations to improve confidence in insights.
Combining machine learning with causal inference to uncover cause-and-effect relationships from materials data.
Using advanced methods like autoencoders and sparse regression to directly extract physical knowledge from noisy experimental data.
papers.abstract:
While the uptake of data-driven approaches for materials science and
chemistry is at an exciting, early stage, to realise the true potential of
machine learning models for successful scientific discovery, they must have
qualities beyond purely predictive power. The predictions and inner workings of
models should provide a certain degree of explainability by human experts,
permitting the identification of potential model issues or limitations,
building trust on model predictions and unveiling unexpected correlations that
may lead to scientific insights. In this work, we summarize applications of
interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and
chemistry and discuss how these techniques can improve the outcome of
scientific studies. We discuss various challenges for interpretable machine
learning in materials science and, more broadly, in scientific settings. In
particular, we emphasize the risks of inferring causation or reaching
generalization by purely interpreting machine learning models and the need of
uncertainty estimates for model explanations. Finally, we showcase a number of
exciting developments in other fields that could benefit interpretability in
material science and chemistry problems.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box by learning the relevance of many-body functions in neural network potentials
papers.research_question: How can neural network potentials (NNPs), specifically coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks, be interpreted by decomposing their inferred energy into n-body interactions to provide human-understandable explanations without compromising predictive power?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends GNN-LRP (Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Graph Neural Networks) to interpret neural network potentials for coarse-grained molecular systems, demonstrating that the decomposed n-body interactions are physically meaningful and consistent across different GNN architectures, thereby enhancing trust in these models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed GNN-LRP method successfully interprets neural network potentials by revealing physically sound many-body interactions, providing a strong argument for trusting and wider adoption of these seemingly black-box models in molecular simulations.
papers.key_findings:
GNN-LRP can decompose the energy output of a neural network potential into interpretable n-body (e.g., 2-body and 3-body) interaction contributions.
For coarse-grained methane, 3-body interactions are negligible, while for water they are significant, aligning with fundamental physical knowledge.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) trained on the same data learn similar underlying physical interactions, as revealed by their relevance attributions.
GNN-LRP can uncover subtle model artifacts in learned interactions that are not detectable through standard molecular dynamics simulation metrics.
Applied to a coarse-grained protein model (NTL9), GNN-LRP identifies stabilizing and destabilizing residue interactions in different metastable states and correctly interprets the effects of mutations.
papers.limitation: Future work is needed to refine these concepts to provide greater insight into ML models and allow researchers to be more systematic in their choice of architecture and functionalization.
future_direction: Apply the interpretation techniques to extract new scientific knowledge on previously unknown systems.
Refine the GNN-LRP concepts to provide greater insight and allow more systematic choices of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials based on artificial neural networks are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One main criticism regarding neural network potentials is that their inferred energy is less interpretable than in traditional approaches, which use simpler and more transparent functional forms. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of explainable artificial intelligence to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks. With these tools, neural network potentials can be practically decomposed into n-body interactions, providing a human understandable interpretation without compromising predictive power. We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. The obtained interpretations suggest that well-trained neural network potentials learn physical interactions, which are consistent with fundamental principles.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: How Do Transformers Learn In-Context Beyond Simple Functions? A Case Study on Learning with Representations
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn in-context beyond simple functions, specifically in the setting of learning with representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows theoretically and empirically that transformers can perform in-context learning with representations, exhibiting mechanisms where lower layers compute the representation and upper layers perform linear in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn in-context with representations and exhibit interpretable mechanisms that align with theoretical constructions.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, transformers can be constructed to implement in-context ridge regression on representations.
Empirically, trained small transformers achieve near-optimal in-context learning risk in supervised and dynamical system settings.
Linear probing reveals that lower layers transform inputs by the representation function, and upper layers perform linear in-context learning on the transformed data.
Copying behaviors of both inputs and representations are observed in the trained transformers.
The upper layers alone, when isolated via pasting experiments, can perform nearly optimal linear in-context learning.
papers.abstract: While large language models based on the transformer architecture have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, understandings of such capabilities are still in an early stage, where existing theory and mechanistic understanding focus mostly on simple scenarios such as learning simple function classes. This paper takes initial steps on understanding ICL in more complex scenarios, by studying learning with representations. Concretely, we construct synthetic in-context learning problems with a compositional structure, where the label depends on the input through a possibly complex but fixed representation function, composed with a linear function that differs in each instance. By construction, the optimal ICL algorithm first transforms the inputs by the representation function, and then performs linear ICL on top of the transformed dataset. We show theoretically the existence of transformers that approximately implement such algorithms with mild depth and size. Empirically, we find trained transformers consistently achieve near-optimal ICL performance in this setting, and exhibit the desired dissection where lower layers transforms the dataset and upper layers perform linear ICL. Through extensive probing and a new pasting experiment, we further reveal several mechanisms within the trained transformers, such as concrete copying behaviors on both the inputs and the representations, linear ICL capability of the upper layers alone, and a post-ICL representation selection mechanism in a harder mixture setting. These observed mechanisms align well with our theory and may shed light on how transformers perform ICL in more realistic scenarios.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Insights Into the Inner Workings of Transformer Models for Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How can explainable AI methods be extended to inspect latent representations in transformer models for protein function prediction, and do the identified relevant sequence parts reflect biological expectations?
papers.core_contribution: Extends integrated gradients to compute head-specific attributions in transformers for protein function prediction, showing that attribution maps correlate with biological sequence annotations and identifying specialized heads.
papers.conclusion: The extended integrated gradients method provides insights into transformer models for protein function prediction, showing that models focus on biologically relevant sequence parts and that specific heads are specialized for certain annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution maps at the embedding layer correlate significantly with UniProt annotations for EC classes and GO membrane term.
Inside the model, specific transformer heads show significant correlation between attributions and annotations, indicating specialization.
For GO membrane term, heads with positive relevance and correlation with transmembrane regions are identified.
For GO catalytic activity, heads correlate with active sites and PROSITE patterns.
The method is sensitive to model parameters and provides insights beyond anecdotal evidence.
papers.limitation: The method may identify significant heads due to coincidental partial alignment of randomly initialized heads with directions in feature space that happen to correlate with sequence annotations.
papers.abstract: Motivation: We explored how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can help to shed light into the inner workings of neural networks for protein function prediction, by extending the widely used XAI method of integrated gradients such that latent representations inside of transformer models, which were finetuned to Gene Ontology term and Enzyme Commission number prediction, can be inspected too. Results: The approach enabled us to identify amino acids in the sequences that the transformers pay particular attention to, and to show that these relevant sequence parts reflect expectations from biology and chemistry, both in the embedding layer and inside of the model, where we identified transformer heads with a statistically significant correspondence of attribution maps with ground truth sequence annotations (e.g. transmembrane regions, active sites) across many proteins. Availability and Implementation: Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/markuswenzel/xai-proteins .

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Operationally meaningful representations of physical systems in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks to learn operationally meaningful representations of physical systems that separate parameters relevant for different experimental settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture that learns operationally meaningful representations of physical systems by imposing a communication efficiency criterion between agents, leading to disentangled parameters that correspond to physically relevant quantities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed architecture can learn operationally meaningful representations that separate physically relevant parameters, and it can be combined with reinforcement learning for interactive settings.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture can separate local parameters from interaction parameters in classical charged particle systems.
It can separate local qubit parameters from quantum correlation parameters in two-qubit systems.
The method can be combined with reinforcement learning to learn representations in interactive scenarios.
future_direction: Combining the method with reinforcement learning for more complex environments.
Exploring other operational criteria for representation learning.
papers.abstract: Abstract To make progress in science, we often build abstract representations of physical systems that meaningfully encode information about the systems. Such representations ignore redundant features and treat parameters such as velocity and position separately because they can be useful for making statements about different experimental settings. Here, we capture this notion by formally defining the concept of operationally meaningful representations. We present an autoencoder architecture with attention mechanism that can generate such representations and demonstrate it on examples involving both classical and quantum physics. For instance, our architecture finds a compact representation of an arbitrary two-qubit system that separates local parameters from parameters describing quantum correlations.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning? Are they essential for pattern matching in ICL?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads are essential for few-shot in-context learning, as their ablation leads to significant performance drops in both abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, and induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying ICL.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of 1% of induction heads leads to substantial ICL performance decreases (up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks).
For NLP tasks, ablation of induction heads reduces the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot performance close to zero-shot.
Attention knockout experiments show that blocking the induction pattern causes performance drops comparable to full head ablations, confirming the specific role of the prefix matching and copying mechanism.
The effects are consistent across two models (Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B).
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of prefix matching and copying for pattern matching.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for induction heads without mechanistic verification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks, not verified across NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL).However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking.This paper explores the role of induction heads in a fewshot ICL setting.We analyse two state-of-theart models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random.For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts.We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present finegrained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: SALSA: Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we learn semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, using SMILES-based autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SALSA, a transformer-autoencoder with a contrastive loss, to learn molecular representations that capture graph-to-graph similarities, resulting in a semantically organized latent space.
papers.conclusion: SALSA learns semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, with improved interpolation and property awareness, and can be applied to other domains with user-defined semantics.
papers.key_findings:
SALSA achieves higher correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance in latent space compared to a naive autoencoder.
SALSA generates more semantically reasonable interpolations between molecules, indicating better semantic continuity.
SALSA implicitly encodes physicochemical properties better than baselines, showing improved property awareness.
The contrastive loss improves structural awareness, while the reconstruction loss acts as a regularizer to prevent degenerative mappings.
SALSA's performance degrades only at very low latent dimensions (e.g., 2 or 4), suggesting robustness down to 8 dimensions.
papers.limitation: The correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance may not hold for molecules that are substantially different
papers.abstract: In deep learning for drug discovery, chemical data are often represented as simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) sequences which allow for straightforward implementation of natural language processing methodologies, one being the sequence-to-sequence autoencoder. However, we observe that training an autoencoder solely on SMILES is insufficient to learn molecular representations that are semantically meaningful, where semantics are defined by the structural (graph-to-graph) similarities between molecules. We demonstrate by example that autoencoders may map structurally similar molecules to distant codes, resulting in an incoherent latent space that does not respect the structural similarities between molecules. To address this shortcoming we propose Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder (SALSA), a transformer-autoencoder modified with a contrastive task, tailored specifically to learn graph-to-graph similarity between molecules. Formally, the contrastive objective is to map structurally similar molecules (separated by a single graph edit) to nearby codes in the latent space. To accomplish this, we generate a novel dataset comprised of sets of structurally similar molecules and opt for a supervised contrastive loss that is able to incorporate full sets of positive samples. We compare SALSA to its ablated counterparts, and show empirically that the composed training objective (reconstruction and contrastive task) leads to a higher quality latent space that is more 1) structurally-aware, 2) semantically continuous, and 3) property-aware.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Symmetry and Generalisation in Neural Approximations of Renormalisation Transformations
papers.research_question: What role do parameter symmetry and network expressivity play in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group transformation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity in neural networks learning renormalization transformations, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalizing poorly. It extends a cumulant propagation framework from MLPs to GNNs to elucidate internal information processing.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that balancing symmetry and expressivity is crucial for generalization in neural networks learning physical transformations, and the cumulant propagation framework offers insight into their internal information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetrically constrained weights in MLPs combined with nonlinear activations (e.g., quadratic) lead to poor generalization, as shown analytically.
Linear networks with symmetric weights generalize well, but adding nonlinearities (ReLU, quadratic) under symmetry constraints degrades generalization.
The independent node approximation for cumulant propagation in GNNs is limited, especially for higher-order cumulants, due to neglected correlations from message passing.
GNNs perform comparably to MLPs on simple two-node graphs but their inductive biases are not beneficial for tasks lacking structural complexity.
Networks with learnable spline activations and fixed weights generalize poorly, while training both weights and splines yields linear solutions that generalize well.
papers.limitation:
The independent node approximation for GNN cumulant propagation is crude and neglects important interactions induced by message passing and weight sharing.
The study is limited to simple network architectures (shallow MLPs and GNNs) and synthetic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the cumulant propagation framework to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigating the role of symmetry breaking in hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have proven enormously successful at using multiple layers of representation to learn relevant features of structured data. Encoding physical symmetries into these models can improve performance on difficult tasks, and recent work has motivated the principle of parameter symmetry breaking and restoration as a unifying mechanism underlying their hierarchical learning dynamics. We evaluate the role of parameter symmetry and network expressivity in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group (RG) transformation, using the central limit theorem (CLT) as a test case map. We consider simple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), and vary weight symmetries and activation functions across architectures.
