Under QLENS, a Transformer is studied by converting its latent activations into a state vector in a Hilbert space derived from the model's output units. This state subsequently evolves through hidden layers - reformulated as unitary operators and analogously defined Hamiltonians - during inference. The model's final probability distribution is obtained by applying the Born rule to the end state using a specific measurement operator. To demonstrate QLENS's potential, we conduct a proof-of-concept by probing a toy Transformer to investigate the influence of individual layers in a model's prediction trajectory. We present our work as a foundation for cross-domain insights to be leveraged towards a broader understanding of Transformers.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What are the precise training dynamics during the emergence of induction heads for in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a simple, interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing induction heads and proves that training dynamics are constrained to a low-dimensional subspace, with only three parameters accounting for the emergence.
papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture. We give a formal proof that the training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace of the parameter space. Empirically, we validate this constraint while observing that only 3 dimensions account for the emergence of an induction head. By further studying the training dynamics inside this 3-dimensional subspace, we find that the time until the emergence of an induction head follows a tight asymptotic bound that is quadratic in the input context length.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Understanding the Staged Dynamics of Transformers in Learning Latent Structure
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn latent structure in a controlled setting, and what are the dynamics of this learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers learn latent structure in discrete stages, first acquiring coarse-grained rules before fine-grained details, and identifies a fundamental asymmetry where composition is robust but decomposition suffers with increasing complexity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers learn latent structure in a coarse-to-fine manner, and exhibit a fundamental asymmetry: they can robustly compose simple rules but struggle to decompose complex examples to discover underlying rules.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns latent structure in interpretable stages: first restricting predictions to the support set (in-support), then identifying the correct half of the structure, and finally pinpointing the exact target.
In composition tasks, the model robustly composes single-step rules to solve multi-step queries without performance degradation as sequence length increases.
In decomposition tasks, increasing the complexity (support hop length) delays learning, primarily by delaying the acquisition of the 'correct half' sub-skill.
An adjacency bias in the latent structure causes the model to learn the exact target before learning the correct half in the partial support task.
The learning dynamics are highly sensitive to hyperparameters; sub-optimal choices can prevent the model from converging or learning specific stages.
papers.limitation: Model performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameter configuration, and sub-optimal choices can prevent the model from learning some stages.
papers.abstract: While transformers can discover latent structure from context, the dynamics of how they acquire different components of the latent structure remain poorly understood. In this work, we use the Alchemy benchmark, to investigate the dynamics of latent structure learning. We train a small decoder-only transformer on three task variants: 1) inferring missing rules from partial contextual information, 2) composing simple rules to solve multi-step sequences, and 3) decomposing complex multi-step examples to infer intermediate steps. By factorizing each task into interpretable events, we show that the model acquires capabilities in discrete stages, first learning the coarse grained rules, before learning the complete latent structure. We also identify a crucial asymmetry, where the model can compose fundamental rules robustly, but struggles to decompose complex examples to discover the fundamental rules. These findings offer new insights into understanding how a transformer model learns latent structures, providing a granular view of how these capabilities evolve during training.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: In-Context Algebra
papers.research_question: What computational strategies do transformers develop when tokens serve as pure variables, acquiring meaning only through their interactions within each sequence, rather than relying on fixed information encoded in token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on an in-context variable assignment task develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms (commutative copying, identity element recognition, closure-based cancellation) that differ from the geometric representations learned in fixed-token arithmetic settings, showing that learned reasoning strategies depend on task structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context about variables whose meanings are not fixed, showing that the kinds of learned strategies are dependent on the task structure.
papers.key_findings:
Models learn a commutative copying mechanism where a dedicated attention head copies answers from previously seen commutative facts.
Models develop an identity element recognition mechanism that distinguishes and solves facts containing the group's identity element.
Models implement a closure-based cancellation mechanism that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers by eliminating impossible variables.
The reasoning strategies learned by transformers are dependent on the task structure, with symbolic, context-based strategies emerging when tokens carry no consistent meaning across contexts.
Models achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and generalize to unseen groups.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on synthetic algebra tasks with small transformer models, which may limit generalizability to larger models or more complex, real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Exploring more complex algebraic structures and reasoning tasks.
Scaling the analysis to larger transformer models.
Investigating whether similar symbolic mechanisms emerge in other in-context learning settings.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms that arise when transformers are trained to solve arithmetic on sequences where tokens are variables whose meaning is determined only through their interactions. While prior work has found that transformers develop geometric embeddings that mirror algebraic structure, those previous findings emerge from settings where arithmetic-valued tokens have fixed meanings. We devise a new task in which the assignment of symbols to specific algebraic group elements varies from one sequence to another. Despite this challenging setup, transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and even generalize to unseen algebraic groups. We develop targeted data distributions to create causal tests of a set of hypothesized mechanisms, and we isolate three mechanisms models consistently learn: commutative copying where a dedicated head copies answers, identity element recognition that distinguishes identity-containing facts, and closure-based cancellation that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers. Complementary to the geometric representations found in fixed-symbol settings, our findings show that models develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context with variables whose meanings are not fixed.

papers.title: Feature Identification via the Empirical NTK
papers.research_question: Whether eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks.
papers.core_contribution: Eigenanalysis of the empirical NTK can recover ground-truth features in toy models, localize features to specific layers, and detect grokking phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: eNTK analysis provides a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.
papers.key_findings:
In Toy Models of Superposition, the eNTK recovers ground-truth features in both sparse and dense regimes.
For a 1-layer MLP trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK recovers Fourier feature families and localizes them to layers; the spectrum develops cliffs that align with the grokking phase transition.
For a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK eigendirections align with Fourier features at key frequencies in specific layers.
Layerwise eNTK can localize features to specific layers.
The evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition.
papers.limitation:
The empirical NTK hypothesis may not hold in general, and its applicability to realistic models is not established.
Experiments are limited to small toy models; it is unclear if the method scales to large models.
future_direction: Understanding analytically the properties leading to clean signals in the eNTK.
Developing unsupervised feature discovery using eNTK eigendirections.
Applying eNTK analysis to larger models like OthelloGPT and realistic LLMs.
papers.abstract: We provide evidence that eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks. Across three standard toy models for mechanistic interpretability, Toy Models of Superposition (TMS), a 1-layer MLP trained on modular addition and a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular addition, we find that top eigenspaces of the eNTK align with ground-truth features. In TMS, the eNTK recovers the ground-truth features in both the sparse (high superposition) and dense regimes. In modular arithmetic, the eNTK can be used to recover Fourier feature families. Moreover, we provide evidence that a layerwise eNTK localizes features to specific layers and that the evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition. These results suggest that eNTK analysis may provide a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Latent Concept Disentanglement in Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformers represent latent structures when performing in-context learning? Do they disentangle and compose latent concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers disentangle and compose latent concepts during in-context learning, representing them in low-dimensional subspaces that reflect the geometry of the latent parameters.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of disentangling and composing latent concepts during in-context learning, with internal representations that capture the geometry of the underlying latent parameters.
papers.key_findings:
For multi-hop reasoning tasks, the model uses step-by-step composition of latent concepts via a sparse set of attention heads.
The bridge-resolving mechanism is much stronger in the larger 27B model compared to the 2B model, indicating model size benefits latent concept disentanglement.
Adding more in-context examples strengthens the causal importance of the relevant sub-circuits and increases concept representation disentanglement.
For numerical tasks with latent parameters, task vectors lie on low-dimensional smooth manifolds that reflect the geometry of the underlying parameter (e.g., radius).
Interpolating along the task vector manifold allows steering the model's computation, approximately interpolating the latent parameter.
papers.limitation:
Only English language queries are used, so mechanisms may differ across languages.
The latent concepts tested are all human-interpretable (e.g., numbers, countries), limiting generalization to more intricate relationships.
papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks for an Accurate and Interpretable Prediction of Material Properties
papers.research_question: How can we develop a machine learning framework that directly learns material properties from the atomic connection in a crystal, providing both accurate predictions and interpretable chemical insights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (CGCNN) framework, which directly learns material properties from crystal graphs, achieving DFT-level accuracy for diverse properties and enabling the extraction of local chemical environment contributions for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The CGCNN framework provides a flexible, accurate, and interpretable method for predicting material properties and extracting design knowledge, as demonstrated by its application to perovskite discovery.
papers.key_findings:
CGCNN achieves prediction accuracy comparable to DFT calculations for eight different material properties using around 10^4 training data points.
The framework is interpretable, allowing extraction of site-specific energy contributions, as demonstrated for perovskite structures.
The learned site energy information can be used to derive empirical rules for material design, significantly reducing the search space for high-throughput screening.
A modified convolution function (Eq. 5) that differentiates interaction strengths between neighbors significantly improves prediction performance over a simpler version (Eq. 4).
CGCNN can predict both continuous properties (e.g., formation energy) and discrete properties (e.g., metal/semiconductor classification) with high accuracy.
papers.limitation: The initial convolution function (Eq. 4) uses a shared weight matrix for all neighbors of an atom, which neglects differences in interaction strength between neighbors.
papers.abstract: The use of machine learning methods for accelerating the design of crystalline materials usually requires manually constructed feature vectors or complex transformation of atom coordinates to input the crystal structure, which either constrains the model to certain crystal types or makes it difficult to provide chemical insights. Here, we develop a crystal graph convolutional neural networks framework to directly learn material properties from the connection of atoms in the crystal, providing a universal and interpretable representation of crystalline materials. Our method provides a highly accurate prediction of density functional theory calculated properties for eight different properties of crystals with various structure types and compositions after being trained with 10^{4} data points. Further, our framework is interpretable because one can extract the contributions from local chemical environments to global properties. Using an example of perovskites, we show how this information can be utilized to discover empirical rules for materials design.

papers.title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers build categorical representations for image classification, and how do self-attention and MLP layers contribute to this process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to project Vision Transformers' internal representations onto the class embedding space, enabling analysis of how class representations are built and the differential roles of self-attention and MLP layers via key-value memory pair mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework is a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability of Vision Transformers, providing insights into their category-building processes.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens develop class-specific representations from early stages, with class identifiability increasing across blocks.
Attention mechanisms and contextual information are crucial for building class representations; image tokens cannot develop class-identifiable representations in isolation.
Self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute: MLP layers promote strong categorical updates in late blocks, while self-attention layers promote weaker but more disseminated updates earlier.
The framework can identify image regions important for class detection and outperforms linear probing in revealing task-relevant features.
Key-value memory pair mechanisms in MLP and self-attention layers are involved in building class representations, with agreement rates correlating with model accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Only studies Vision Transformers trained for image classification.
Does not explore model editing or performance improvement applications.
future_direction: Adapt the framework to models with other types of output embeddings.
Use the mechanistic insights for model editing or performance improvement.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing use of transformer models in computer vision, a mechanistic understanding of these networks is still needed. This work introduces a method to reverse-engineer Vision Transformers trained to solve image classification tasks. Inspired by previous research in NLP, we demonstrate how the inner representations at any level of the hierarchy can be projected onto the learned class embedding space to uncover how these networks build categorical representations for their predictions. We use our framework to show how image tokens develop class-specific representations that depend on attention mechanisms and contextual information, and give insights on how self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute to this categorical composition. We additionally demonstrate that this method (1) can be used to determine the parts of an image that would be important for detecting the class of interest, and (2) exhibits significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. Taken together, our results position our proposed framework as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability research.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Binary and Ternary Transformers
papers.research_question: Do binary and ternary transformer networks learn distinctly different or similar algorithms compared to full-precision transformer networks for modular addition?
papers.core_contribution: Binary and ternary transformers learn similar Fourier-based algorithms as full-precision transformers for modular addition, providing evidence against their use as more interpretable alternatives.
papers.conclusion: Binary and ternary transformers learn similar algorithms to full-precision transformers for modular addition and are not more interpretable, with binary models showing more noise in analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Binary and ternary networks exhibit grokking behavior similar to full-precision networks when weight decay regularization is applied.
Binary and ternary models learn similar periodic patterns in embeddings and logits as full-precision models.
Binary models show more noise in Fourier analysis compared to full-precision models.
Ternary models behave intermediately between binary and full-precision models but do not achieve superior loss.
No evidence was found that binary or ternary networks learn simpler, more interpretable discrete algorithms.
papers.limitation:
Lack of conclusive evidence concerning exactly what algorithm was learned, since many different algorithms could be learned for modular addition.
The implementation did not binarize/ternarize the embed and unembed layers, limiting the study to partially binarized networks.
Only the most basic straight-through estimator technique was explored for optimizing binary/ternary networks.
future_direction: Explore more complicated techniques for optimizing binary and ternary networks using mechanistic interpretability.
Investigate fully binarized/ternarized networks in all layers.
Investigate whether binary and ternary networks always learn similar algorithms for other toy problems or in language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research (arXiv:2310.11453, arXiv:2402.17764) has proposed binary and ternary transformer networks as a way to significantly reduce memory and improve inference speed in Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining accuracy. In this work, we apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to investigate whether such networks learn distinctly different or similar algorithms when compared to full-precision transformer networks. In particular, we reverse engineer the algorithms learned for the toy problem of modular addition where we find that binary and ternary networks learn similar algorithms as full precision networks. This provides evidence against the possibility of using binary and ternary networks as a more interpretable alternative in the LLM setting.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: In-Context Learning Without Copying
papers.research_question: Are induction heads a necessary building block for learning abstractive in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, or can such capabilities emerge independently?
papers.core_contribution: Abstractive in-context learning capabilities can emerge independently of induction heads, as demonstrated by the HAPAX training regime which suppresses inductive copying but preserves abstractive ICL performance.
papers.conclusion: The developmental link between induction heads and abstractive in-context learning capabilities is weaker than previously hypothesized.
papers.key_findings:
HAPAX training reduces inductive copying by 66% on random repetition tasks.
Abstractive ICL capabilities are preserved under HAPAX, with the model achieving higher accuracy on 13 out of 21 tasks.
Models trained with HAPAX develop fewer and weaker induction heads.
The token-loss difference metric is primarily affected by exact copying and does not correlate well with abstractive ICL capabilities.
Previous token heads can lead to prefix-matching patterns even in randomly initialized attention heads.
papers.abstract: Induction heads are attention heads that perform inductive copying by matching patterns from earlier context and copying their continuations verbatim. As models develop induction heads, they experience a sharp drop in training loss, a phenomenon cited as evidence that induction heads may underlie a wide range of in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. In this work, we investigate whether induction heads are a necessary building block for learning abstractive ICL capabilities (i.e., tasks where the answer is not contained in the input context), or whether such capabilities can emerge independently. We propose Hapax, a training regime that omits the loss contribution of tokens predictable by induction heads. Despite a significant reduction in inductive copying, abstractive ICL capabilities are preserved, with the model achieving higher accuracy than the vanilla model on 13 out of 21 tasks, even though 31.7% of tokens are omitted from the loss. Furthermore, our model achieves lower loss values on token positions that induction heads cannot predict. Mechanistic analysis shows that models trained with Hapax develop fewer and weaker induction heads despite preserving abstractive ICL capabilities. Our findings suggest that the developmental link between induction heads and abstractive ICL capabilities is weaker than previously hypothesized.

papers.title: LyTimeT: Towards Robust and Interpretable State-Variable Discovery
papers.research_question: How to extract true dynamical variables from high-dimensional video data robustly and interpretably, despite distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LyTimeT, a two-phase framework that combines global spatio-temporal attention with Lyapunov-based stability regularization to learn robust, interpretable latent representations of dynamical systems from video.
papers.conclusion: LyTimeT bridges representation learning and stability theory, providing a principled foundation for robust, generalizable, and scientifically meaningful modeling of complex dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth compared to baselines like NSV and TIDE.
LyTimeT delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based and transformer-only baselines.
LyTimeT remains invariant under background perturbations, demonstrating robustness to nuisance variation.
Lyapunov regularization improves MI, lowers AMSE, and reduces long-horizon error, enhancing stability and interpretability.
LyTimeT-Lite variant maintains near-optimal performance with lower computational cost, suitable for real-time deployment.
future_direction: Incorporating physics-informed priors such as symplectic structures, conservation laws, or energy-preserving constraints.
Investigating hierarchical and sparse attention mechanisms to scale to higher-resolution videos and partially observed systems.
Exploring online or continual learning to adapt latent variables in evolving environments for closed-loop control applications.
papers.abstract: Extracting the true dynamical variables of a system from high-dimensional video is challenging due to distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes. We propose LyTimeT, a two-phase framework for interpretable variable extraction that learns robust and stable latent representations of dynamical systems. In Phase 1, LyTimeT employs a spatio-temporal TimeSformer-based autoencoder that uses global attention to focus on dynamically relevant regions while suppressing nuisance variation, enabling distraction-robust latent state learning and accurate long-horizon video prediction. In Phase 2, we probe the learned latent space, select the most physically meaningful dimensions using linear correlation analysis, and refine the transition dynamics with a Lyapunov-based stability regularizer to enforce contraction and reduce error accumulation during roll-outs. Experiments on five synthetic benchmarks and four real-world dynamical systems, including chaotic phenomena, show that LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth, remains invariant under background perturbations, and delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based (TIDE) and transformer-only baselines. Our results demonstrate that combining spatio-temporal attention with stability constraints yields predictive models that are not only accurate but also physically interpretable.

papers.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is in-context learning (ICL) in transformers a persistent phenomenon, or does it emerge and then disappear (become transient) during training?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning (ICL) in transformers is often transient: it emerges and then disappears during training, even as training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for in-weights learning (IWL).
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is often transient, emphasizing the importance of validation metrics, early stopping, or regularization to preserve ICL capabilities during training.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges and then disappears (is transient) during training, while IWL accuracy increases.
ICL transience occurs across a range of model sizes (depth, embedding dimension), dataset sizes (number of classes, exemplars per class), and dataset types (Omniglot images, LLaMa token embeddings).
Data distributional properties, such as a larger number of classes or a Zipfian skew, can postpone the transience of ICL.
L2 regularization can mitigate or eliminate ICL transience, potentially by favoring the lower-norm ICL circuit.
Preliminary evidence suggests ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits for resources in the transformer's residual stream.
future_direction: Explore the effect of alternate optimizers or initialization schemes on the transience of ICL.
Connect findings to natural language settings and large-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to "overtrain" transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

papers.title: Attribute Graphs Underlying Molecular Generative Models: Path to Learning with Limited Data
papers.research_question: How can we extract a graphical model (attribute graph) relating data attributes from the latent representations of a pre-trained generative model, and use this structure for robust prediction with limited out-of-distribution data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PerturbLearn, a method to extract an attribute graph (a DAG) from a pre-trained generative autoencoder by perturbing latent codes and observing influences on data attributes, and shows that using the Markov blanket from this graph for feature selection leads to robust prediction under distribution shifts with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The PerturbLearn framework successfully extracts a graphical model from a pre-trained generative model, and using this structure for feature selection enables more robust and generalizable predictors in scenarios with limited out-of-distribution data.
papers.key_findings:
The attribute graph derived by PerturbLearn captures latent-mediated influences among molecular attributes.
Predictors using the Markov blanket features from the PerturbLearn graph show better generalization and robustness to distribution shifts, especially when fine-tuning data is limited (e.g., n=7, 10, 25 samples).
The method is competitive with or outperforms existing causal discovery (GES, LiNGAM) and feature selection methods (Sparse Group Lasso, PPFS) in low-data regimes across multiple pharmacokinetic property prediction tasks.
The derived graphical model provides a means for sample-efficient domain adaptation and offers (partial) interpretability by identifying relevant attributes.
papers.limitation: Dependency on a pre-determined set of data attributes, which may not be comprehensive.
future_direction: Further investigation on the accordance of the derived attribute graph with domain priors.
Using only low-level and cheaply computable attributes.
Incorporating expert knowledge.
papers.abstract: Training generative models that capture rich semantics of the data and interpreting the latent representations encoded by such models are very important problems in un-/self-supervised learning. In this work, we provide a simple algorithm that relies on perturbation experiments on latent codes of a pre-trained generative autoencoder to uncover an attribute graph that is implied by the generative model. We perform perturbation experiments to check for influence of a given latent variable on a subset of attributes. Given this, we show that one can fit an effective graphical model that models a structural equation model between latent codes taken as exogenous variables and attributes taken as observed variables. One interesting aspect is that a single latent variable controls multiple overlapping subsets of attributes unlike conventional approaches that try to impose full independence.
